families.s: HSE textile-industry health-surveillance and early-intervention guidance
families.t: systematic checks, early signs, risk-based methods, control failure, worker reporting, records, referral and review
f: Health surveillance consists of systematic regular checks to identify early signs of work-related ill health.
The method should be proportionate to the health risks from the job.
Surveillance can protect workers who are at increased risk.
Early detection allows treatment and action to prevent further harm.
Results can warn that exposure controls are no longer effective.
Health surveillance does not replace elimination or control of the hazard.
Workers may fail to report symptoms, so a planned system is needed where the legal criteria are met.
Abnormal results should trigger confidential follow-up, review of controls and appropriate work adjustments.
families.g: Surveillance need depends on the harmful agent or process, residual exposure, identifiable disease, valid detection methods, worker susceptibility, control performance and follow-up arrangements.

families.s: HSE textile-laundry and dry-cleaning respiratory-hazard guidance
families.t: chlorine, hypochlorite, ammonia, sulphur dioxide, filter powder, contaminated laundry, dust, ventilation, RPE and exposure control
f: Laundry and dry-cleaning workers can inhale chlorine, hypochlorite, ammonia, sulphur dioxide and filter-powder contaminants.
Contaminated laundry can introduce additional hazardous dusts and fibres.
Textile process dust and reactive dye powders can cause respiratory irritation and occupational asthma.
Exposure to fumes, dusts and airborne chemicals should be controlled at source.
Powder handling should minimise dust generation and dispersion.
Suitable respiratory protection may be required where adequate control cannot otherwise be achieved.
Health surveillance may be needed where residual exposure presents a recognised respiratory risk.
COSHH assessment should cover chemical products, mixing, leaks, ventilation, cleaning, storage, spills and maintenance.
families.g: Laundry and dry-cleaning respiratory risk depends on chemicals and contaminated textiles, process temperature, mixing and dosing, ventilation, dust generation, maintenance, PPE and worker susceptibility.

families.s: HSE plastics-machine safeguarding and intervention guidance
families.t: injection, blow moulding, thermoforming, extrusion, guarding, interlocks, isolation, cleaning, maintenance and competent intervention
f: Plastics-sector machine guidance covers injection moulding, blow moulding, thermoforming and extruder lines.
Practical safeguards should prevent access to dangerous machine movements during production.
Interlocked guards are needed where regular access is foreseeable and danger can persist.
Machine interventions such as clearing, setting, cleaning and maintenance require safe systems.
Energy sources should be isolated and stored energy controlled before entering danger zones.
Safeguarding should reflect the machine's age, design, movement and foreseeable misuse.
Operators and maintenance staff need task-specific information and competence.
Defeated guards, damaged interlocks and recurring access problems should lead to immediate corrective action.
families.g: Plastics-machine risk depends on machine type, clamping and cutting forces, hot material, access frequency, guarding and interlocks, stored energy, intervention method, maintenance and competence.

families.t: mould area, clamp movement, guards, interlocks, purging, hot polymer, nozzle, setting, maintenance and isolation
f: HSE publishes specific practical safeguarding guidance for injection moulding machines.
The mould and clamp area presents crushing and trapping hazards.
Guards and interlocks should prevent dangerous movement while access openings are exposed.
Purging and nozzle work can expose workers to hot polymer and unexpected discharge.
Setting and fault finding should use reduced-risk modes and controlled access.
Maintenance should include inspection and testing of guards, interlocks and control systems.
Isolation is required before work that enters or reaches into dangerous areas.
Process temperature, pressure, material condition and decomposition products should be included in the task assessment.
families.g: Injection-moulding risk depends on clamp force and movement, guard design, hot polymer and pressure, purging, access, control mode, isolation, maintenance and operator competence.

families.t: mould movement, extrusion head, parison, cutting, compressed air, hot plastic, guarding, access and maintenance
f: HSE provides machine-specific safeguards for blow moulding machines.
Closing moulds and moving platens create crushing and trapping hazards.
Extrusion heads, parison cutters and hot plastic create burn and cutting hazards.
Compressed-air systems and blowing operations add stored-energy and ejection risks.
Guards and interlocks should prevent access during dangerous movement.
Clearing jams and removing malformed products should follow a defined safe system.
Maintenance and adjustment should be performed under secure isolation where access to danger zones is needed.
Control-system faults or defeated safeguards should stop production until corrected.
families.g: Blow-moulding risk depends on mould and platen movement, hot material, cutters, compressed air, access and ejection, guards and controls, isolation, maintenance and competence.
